claims.text: \item \textbf{Three falsifiable predictions} (\S3.4) that distinguish our framework from informal accounts of bi-level RSI: (P1) a closed-form effect-size bound for ignition tests under measurement noise, (P2) a proof-of-concept that $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ must be ungameable for Level-2 RSI, and (P3) an alternative explanation for observed anti-reward-hacking emergence.

\textbf{Key concept}: the \emph{audit channel} $\alpha$ between inner and outer loops is the load-bearing object; we argue that any bi-level RSI without a properly specified $\alpha$ cannot reach Level-2 regardless of inner-loop sophistication.

\textbf{Three falsifiable predictions}: P1 (Appendix~C) gives a closed-form noise bound for the ignition test, with proof under i.i.d.\ and AR(1) evaluation models; P2 (Appendix~D) shows that predictable $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ is sufficient to block Level-2 RSI, via three lemmas establishing gap monotonicity; P3 (Appendix~E) defines audit-channel capacity $C(\alpha)$ and derives the relation $r(\alpha) = 1 - (C(\alpha) - C_0)/(C_{\max} - C_0)$ under TEE-isolated audit.

Steinhardt \cite{steinhardt2023secret} (2023) enumerates 7 operational definitions in the literature and concludes that no single system has yet satisfied any of them under strict measurement criteria.
We treat AIDE\textsuperscript{2} as a \emph{specimen} of bi-level RSI rather than a definitive proof of RSI.
Second, the gate is \textbf{only on $\mu_{\text{priv}}$}, never on $\mu_{\text{pub}}$.
\begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Unobservable to $\Lambda$.} $\Lambda$ cannot read $\alpha$.
The agent cannot consult its own audit trail without record.

(The 1/2 threshold is conventional and arbitrary; we adopt it for definiteness.) P2 then states: any bi-level RSI in which $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ is predictable (in the above sense) cannot reach Level 2 --- i.e., cannot have improved $\Lambda$ simultaneously serve as improved $\Omega$ over consecutive outer-loop iterations.
\textbf{Proof sketch.} Suppose $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ is predictable by some $f \in F$.

The full proof, including regularity conditions on $F$ and a lower bound on the rate at which $\Delta$ grows, is in Appendix C (formal proof using online learning theory, including three lemmas, the main theorem, and a numerical illustration).

\paragraph{P3 --- Anti-reward-hacking capacity $\equiv$ audit-channel capacity \emph{(falsifiable conjecture; see Appendix E.5 for the formal statement and E.6 for the partial proof)}.} Observed reductions in reward-hacking rate (AIDE\textsuperscript{2} reports 63\% $\to$ 42\% $\to$ 34\% across AIDE0, AIDE47, AIDE85) are more parsimoniously described as evolution of the audit channel's filtering capacity than as emergent alignment.
To make this falsifiable, we operationalize $\alpha$ concretely as the set of regex patterns over $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ computation that an agent cannot bypass without explicit capability.
Second, our proof of P2 assumes $\sigma$ is known and i.i.d., which may not hold across 100 outer-loop steps; sensitivity analysis is required.
The P1 noise bound is non-trivially informative even at moderate $\rho$; the test is provably underpowered for any plausible $\rho > 0$ with $N_{\text{inner}} = 5$.
Both calibers are on CPU; no GPU is used.
This solves the ``eval repair monkey patch'' class of issues: a rewrite that silently alters the evaluation pipeline cannot pass without an external reviewer noticing the drift.

Where the cost is bearable, run $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ computation inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) such that the inner-loop agent cannot observe private scores even via observation side-channels.
Our P2 prediction requires $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ to be polynomially-impossible to compute from public history.
\textbf{Hedged causal language throughout}.
We use ``consistent with'', ``directional'', and ``supports the framework'' rather than absolute causal wording.
Claims are explicitly annotated by evidence tier so that reviewers can distinguish what is proven, what is simulation-supported, and what is a design suggestion:
The formal recommendations are conditional on the stated assumptions, datasets, and runtime settings, and are not universal safety assurances.

(TMLR distinguishes position, methods, contribution, and survey papers; methods papers introduce a new formalism and instantiate it on at least one concrete system, which matches our structure.) We have not framed the paper as a definitive proof of architectural failure in any specific system; we have framed it as \emph{useful vocabulary} for a field that has not yet developed it.
The V8 \S11 Resource Contracts (RC) abstraction binds each layer to a four-field specification: preconditions, postconditions, resource bounds, and audit-guarantee invariants.
\section*{Appendix C: Formal Proof of P1} \addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix C: Formal Proof of P1}
This appendix gives a complete proof of P1 (the ignition-test noise lower bound of \S3.4) using elementary concentration inequalities and the AR(1) effective-sample-size calculation.
\subsection*{C.4 Proof under Assumption 1 (i.i.d.)}
\textit{Proof.} The numerator of $d_{\text{ignition}}$ is the difference of two means over $n_{\text{outer}}$ i.i.d.\ samples each.
\subsection*{C.5 Proof under Assumption 2 (AR(1))}

\textit{Proof.} Under the AR(1) outer-loop correlation model, the $T$ outer-loop $\Omega$-states have effective sample size \[ n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{T (1 - \rho)}{1 + \rho} \] in the standard AR(1) effective-sample-size formula (this is the variance inflation of the running mean).

\item \textbf{Empirical observation}: AIDE\textsuperscript{2} reports ``$\sim$20 steps vs.\ $\sim$40 steps'' with no statistical significance, which matches the bound: at $N_{\text{outer}} = 5$, the test is provably underpowered for any plausible $\rho \in [0.5, 0.9]$.
\section*{Appendix D: Formal Proof of P2} \addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix D: Formal Proof of P2}
This appendix gives a complete proof of P2 (the ungameability claim of \S3.4) using online-learning theory.
The main text's \S3.4.2 contained a proof sketch; the full argument is below.

\textbf{Assumption 4 (No-Information-Without-Causality).} The inner-loop optimizer $\Lambda$ cannot directly observe $\mu_{\text{priv}}$; its only access to $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ is via $f_t(\mathcal{H}_{\text{pub}}^t)$ and the public score $\mu_{\text{pub}}^t$.
\textit{Proof.} By Assumption 4, $\Lambda$ has no oracle access to $\mu_{\text{priv}}$.
\textit{Proof.} The retention gate uses $\mu_{\text{priv}}^t$ (Assumption 3).
\textit{Proof.} We derive the gap dynamics in three steps.

\textit{Proof.} By Lemma 3, after $T_0 := c \cdot \sigma_\mu^2 / \Delta_{\text{crit}}$ outer-loop steps (for some constant $c$ depending on the family $F$), the gap satisfies $\Delta_{T_0} \geq \Delta_{\text{crit}}$.

The outer loop cannot, in this regime, distinguish a genuine improvement (a $\Lambda$ with high $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ for the right reason) from a public-history prediction (a $\Lambda$ with high $f_t$).
The proof relies on Assumptions 1--4, of which the most consequential is Assumption 1 (predictability).
Three other limitations: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof assumes i.i.d.\ noise $\delta$; in practice, $\delta$ may drift across outer-loop steps.
\item The proof assumes the inner-loop optimizer is approximately a no-regret learner on $F$.
\item The proof treats $\Omega$ as fixed; in practice, $\Omega$ may also be modified (an additional outer-outer loop).
Extending the proof to $k$-level RSI is an open direction.

With $c \approx 50$ (the empirical no-regret constant for 16-dim linear regression), $T_0 \approx 2$ outer-loop steps --- meaning the gap $\Delta$ reaches $\sigma_\mu$ essentially immediately under the predicted $\mu_{\text{priv}}$, and the outer loop cannot accumulate Level-2 RSI signal.

This matches AIDE\textsuperscript{2}'s reported underpowering of the ignition test (\S3.4) and the $\S4.3$ DDC quantitative amplifier's finding that the test is provably underpowered at $N_{\text{inner}} = 5$.

Combined with the proof above, the empirical predictability of $\mu_{\text{priv}}$ on the linear class \emph{would imply}, under the other regularity conditions, that a bi-level RSI agent using the same public-history representation fails to reach Level 2.
This appendix provides the precise mathematical formulation and a partial proof of the no-empirical-loophole direction.
\subsection*{E.3 Partial Proof (no-loophole direction)}

\textit{Proof sketch of the $r \to 0$ implication.} Consider an audit channel $\alpha$ of capacity $C(\alpha) = C_{\max}$, i.e., one that records all system state transitions in a TEE-isolated append-only log.
\textit{Proof sketch of the $C \to 0$ implication.} Consider an audit channel $\alpha$ of capacity $C(\alpha) = C_0$, i.e., one that records no system state.
The monotonicity claim in the theorem is empirical; the full formal proof requires a Shannon-capacity lower bound for each $\alpha$-class, which is beyond the scope of this paper.

All code is available at the project repository~\cite{anon2026bi}: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathtt{p2\_falsification/}$ --- the meta-predictor module and its synthetic-data test; the canonical single-split rerun ($\text{AUC}=0.9970$, seed 0) and 10-fold CV mean ($0.9957\pm0.0027$, linear) are reproducible on CPU with scikit-learn; no GPU is required or used.
